#!/bin/bash
# old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...
#
# Runs the old code, the base's: bin/fortress of the batch's one base build, with FORTRESS_HOME set to the
# base build and FORTRESS_CACHES to a private caches folder. If the folder does not exist yet, it is first
# made as a copy of the base build's default_repository/caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). The paths in those caches
# are the base build's own, so nothing is translated, and no worktree is made.
#
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss    the compiled path: compile ...
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P            ... then run
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss            walk
#
# Every cache a run writes goes to the private folder: every cache directory and the logs are under
# fortress.caches (repository/ProjectProperties.java:283-299), which FORTRESS_CACHES sets, and
# bin/fortress_classpath and bin/run_classpath put FORTRESS_CACHES/bytecode_cache on the class path.
# Under the base build a run reads the build, the library sources and default_repository/configuration, and
# writes nothing that stays: the parser writes its error logs beside each file it parses from source and
# deletes them (compiler/Parser.java:349-367), so a compile of a program that exports Executable creates and
# deletes two empty, gitignored logs beside Library/Executable.fsi. Two runs at once may share those two
# names; that is harmless, because the base's library parses without errors, so both logs stay empty and
# a log removed by the other run reads as empty (Parser.java:373-377). Measured in
# explorations/coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md, section 6.
#
# Keep the private folder and your programs outside the base build (the program's own logs go beside it).
# Refuses (exit 2) a base build that is not built, and a private folder inside the base build.
set -euo pipefail
USAGE='usage: old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...'
BASE=$(realpath "${1:?$USAGE}")
PRIV_ARG=${2:?$USAGE}
shift 2
[ -x "$BASE/bin/fortress" ] && [ -e "$BASE/ProjectFortress/build/com/sun/fortress/Shell.class" ] \
  && [ -e "$BASE/default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar" ] \
  || { echo "old-fortress: $BASE is not a built tree" >&2 ; exit 2 ; }
PRIV=$(realpath -m "$PRIV_ARG")
case "$PRIV/" in "$BASE"/*) echo "old-fortress: $PRIV is inside the base build $BASE" >&2 ; exit 2 ;; esac
if [ ! -d "$PRIV" ]; then
    mkdir -p "$(dirname "$PRIV")"
    PART="$PRIV.part.$$"
    cp -a "$BASE/default_repository/caches" "$PART"
    mv -T "$PART" "$PRIV" 2>/dev/null || rm -rf "$PART"     # another run made it first: use that one
fi
FORTRESS_HOME="$BASE" FORTRESS_CACHES="$PRIV" exec "$BASE/bin/fortress" "$@"

(* c18: building a Map[\String, Array2\] whose values are matrices of DIFFERENT
   shapes.  A map comprehension fails inside the library's covariant
   collection ("Singleton[(FlatString,__DefaultMatrix[RR64,16,16])] APPCOV
   Singleton[(FlatString,__DefaultMatrix[RR64,64,16])] have no common
   supertype", build/Check.fss run of 2026-09-09).  Three alternatives:
   (a) a list comprehension of pairs with an explicit static argument, fed to
       mapping();  (b) BIG UNION over singleton maps with explicit static
       arguments;  (c) a sequential fold with add. *)
component c18_map_of_shapes
import List.{...}
import Map.{...}
export Executable

shape(name: String): (ZZ32, ZZ32) = if name = "a" then (2, 3) elif name = "b" then (4, 3) else (3, 5) end
make(name: String): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do (n, m) = shape(name); array[\RR64\](n, m).fill(1.0) end
nm = <|[\String\] "a", "b", "c" |>

run(): () = do
  (* (c) fold *)
  var mc: Map[\String, Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\]\] := {[\String, Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\]\] }
  for name <- seq(nm) do mc := mc.add(name, make(name)) end
  println("(c) fold: " (dom(mc)) " sizes " <| (mc[k]).sizes | k <- nm |>)
  (* (b) BIG UNION of singleton maps *)
  mb = BIG UNION[\String, Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\]\][name <- nm] {[\String, Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\]\] name |-> make(name) }
  println("(b) BIG UNION: " (dom(mb)) " sizes " <| (mb[k]).sizes | k <- nm |>)
  (* (a) list of pairs with a static argument, then mapping *)
  pairs = <|[\(String, Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\])\] (name, make(name)) | name <- nm |>
  ma = mapping[\String, Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\]\](pairs)
  println("(a) mapping(pairs): " (dom(ma)) " sizes " <| (ma[k]).sizes | k <- nm |>)
  (* (d) the map comprehension itself, with static arguments, for the record *)
  md = {[\String, Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\]\] name |-> make(name) | name <- nm }
  println("(d) comprehension: " (dom(md)))
end
end

content.content:
- F-83 **In the interpreter's library, the string components `String.fss` and `FlatString.fss` hold no site of the distance, the compiled checker's errors in that library (F-53), and the rung's repairs of their refused declarations are in forms that the library already uses.** The trait `String` is declared in `FortressLibrary`, not in `String.fss`, which holds string objects and traits such as `CatString` and `SubString`. `String`'s api writes `abstract` on the members its component's trait leaves without a body or does not declare, and its `excludes` clause is the component's (F-286), so `String` has no entry in the `FortressLibrary` export error. `FlatString`'s api declares its component's header, `extends { String, DelegatedIndexed[\Char, ZZ32\] }`, and no `opr ||(a:FlatString, self)` (F-259). Open library bugs: `FlatString.rangeContains` finds only the first occurrence of the character, and so does `CatString`'s, through its flat halves (row 607). An implicit strided subscript `[:b:c]` is completed from the axis's right end, not from its left as `l:b:c`: `"abcdef"[:3:2]` is `bd`, not `ac` (row 609; the expected failure `tests/XXXSubscriptImplicitStridedRange.fss` holds the specification's answer). Gated by `tests/StringPieces.fss`, which pins row 607's two wrong `false` answers. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-string-slips/REPORT.md` sections 4 and 8.

- F-286 **The api's `String` writes `abstract` on every member that its component's trait leaves without a body, and every string object defines them.** `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:2583-2658` writes 14 of `String`'s members `abstract`: `size`, `depth`, `asFlatString`, `isBalanced`, `verify`, `asDebugStringIndented`, `get`, `uncheckedSubstring`, `rangeContains`, `splitWithOffsets`, `split`, `balanced`, `opr ||(self, c:Char)` and `writeOn`. The component's trait (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4507-4643`) declares all 14, none with a body. `FlatString`, `CatString`, `EmptyString` and `SubString` each define all 14 under walk. `String`'s `excludes` clause is `{ Number, Char, AnyMultiplicativeRing }` on both sides; `AnyList` states its exclusion of `String` itself (`Library/List.fsi:55`). So `String` has no entry in the `FortressLibrary` export error (F-282). `CatString`'s `rangeContains` answers what its flat halves answer, so it carries row 607's miss. Gated by `ProjectFortress/tests/StringMembersPromisedWalk.fss` and by the distance stage's per-site list. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-string-members/REPORT.md`, sections 1, 2 and 5.

- F-249 **Under walk, a program that imports only the prelude reaches the string objects' own `||` through the top-level `opr ||(a:String, b:String)`, whose `typecase` calls them.** The string objects' own `||` are those that the objects `FlatString` and `EmptyString` declare, and that the trait `Concatenable` declares for the objects `CatString` and `SubString`. `FortressLibrary`, where the top-level `||` is declared, sees them only where an api that it imports states them: `FlatString`'s api does, and String's api states `Concatenable`'s and `EmptyString`'s three each (`Library/String.fsi:17-19`, `:29-31`). So `"s" || "t"` is a `FlatString` of depth 0, as it was while `String`'s abstract `opr ||(self, b:String)` stood (F-276); a top-level meet with `Concatenable`'s body, which a probe tried, gave a `CatString` of depth 1. Gated by `tests/StringConcatenationFamiliesWalk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-symbolic-library/REPORT.md` section 12, decision 3; `perf-probes/symbolic-operators/REPORT.md` sections 2.2 and 2.4.

- F-253 **Under walk, a call of a generic method that writes no static argument infers the method's own static arguments from the arguments' run-time types.** This holds for a dotted call, as for a call of a generic function, whether the method is alone under its name or among its receiver's overloads. Among the receiver's overloads, where one of two is a generic dotted method and exactly one of their declared domains lies inside the other, walk chooses the inner one; otherwise it compares them on the instance that the call makes (F-252). A generic method that a trait declares reads its bounds, and the types to which its arguments convert, in the trait's method environment, where its instances bind and evaluate their types, as a method that an object declares does. So it takes the instance that the same method declared in an object takes: a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` give `Box[\ZZ64\]` with the `ZZ32` converted, and a bounded type parameter that nothing fixes takes its bound. A generic functional method that an object inherits from a trait is chosen beside the object's plain one where only it applies. Where the inference with conversion finds no instance, as for an argument outside a bound, walk falls back to unification. For a trait's method, the unification still reads the trait's member environment, which has no parent, as the team's code did. So it does not read the bound, and the call fails with 'Cannot unify Int ... with Shape ... abm=K=(Int,Any)'; the same method declared in an object fails with 'Meet(Int, Shape) not a singleton'. This inference lets the team's generic `distribute` over `K` run nested reductions under walk (F-248). Gated by `tests/MethodStaticArgInference.fss`, `MethodStaticArgOverloadedReceiver.fss`, `MethodStaticArgDeclaredDomain.fss`, `NestedReductionFusion.fss`, `TraitGenericMethodInference.fss` and `InheritedGenericFunctionalMethodBesidePlain.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-method-sargs/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 2; `compile-ladder/rung-walk-trait-method-bounds/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 4, and its `SKEPTIC.md` section 3.

- F-123 **A compiled object with no `asString` of its own prints its bare type name, as walk does.** A value whose run-time Java class declares its own `toString`, such as the compiled `RR32`'s, prints by it. Open on the compiled path: through the prelude's `Object`, an object that declares or inherits a zero-argument Fortress member named `toString` overflows the stack when it is printed (row 321), though not through the one library's `Object`, whose `asString` is `self.ilkName`; and `asDebugString` and `asExprString` print differently from walk's, where the specification is silent (row 363). For a string static argument walk is the one that is wrong: it takes the argument from the run-time class, so `Cell("s")` prints `Cell[\FlatString\]`, where the compiled `Cell[\String\]` is the specification's answer (row 364). For a numeral argument neither path gives the specification's type. Gated by `compiler_tests/DefaultRenderRungS`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-default-rendering/REPORT.md`, "Defects and their homes".
